brief.summary: Analysis software for freelance back-of-book indexers that shows the structure of a draft index against the book's pages, so they can find imbalances and errors before delivering it to the publisher.
brief.user: Corinne Ashdown, a self-employed indexer with fifteen years of work for university presses. She works alone from home, bills by the indexable page, and takes about four books a month in busy season.
brief.moment: Corinne has finished a first-pass index for a 612-page history of Atlantic whaling ports and has four days left before delivery. She's going through it for structural problems the publisher's editor will catch: main entries with long runs of undifferentiated page locators, chapters that are under-indexed relative to their length, cross-references that point to nothing or loop, and names indexed inconsistently ('New Bedford' vs 'New Bedford, Mass.'). She wants to see where locators cluster against the chapter structure and drill into the chapters that look thin, then decide which entries to break into subentries, given the publisher's length limit.
brief.data: Draft index: 3,840 main entries, 9,215 subentries, 21,470 page locators, 412 'see' and 'see also' cross-references. Book: 612 pages in 14 chapters plus notes (pp. 541–598) and bibliography. Each entry has heading, subentries, locators (single pages and ranges like 233–41), entry type (person, place, ship, concept), and count of locators. Known issues so far: 96 entries with more than 7 undifferentiated locators, the largest being 'whale oil' with 38. Chapter 9 (pp. 301–344) has about half the locator density of neighbouring chapters. 7 cross-references go to missing headings, and 1 loop runs 'sperm whaling' → 'whaling, sperm' → back. The publisher allows 28 typeset pages at about 110 lines per page, and the current estimate is 31.5 pages. The fee is $4.10 per indexable page.

I need the front end for Indexwright. Analysis software for freelance back-of-book indexers that shows the structure of a draft index against the book's pages, so they can find imbalances and errors before delivering it to the publisher.

Who's using it: Corinne Ashdown, a self-employed indexer with fifteen years of work for university presses. She works alone from home, bills by the indexable page, and takes about four books a month in busy season.

What they're doing right now: Corinne has finished a first-pass index for a 612-page history of Atlantic whaling ports and has four days left before delivery. She's going through it for structural problems the publisher's editor will catch: main entries with long runs of undifferentiated page locators, chapters that are under-indexed relative to their length, cross-references that point to nothing or loop, and names indexed inconsistently ('New Bedford' vs 'New Bedford, Mass.'). She wants to see where locators cluster against the chapter structure and drill into the chapters that look thin, then decide which entries to break into subentries, given the publisher's length limit.

What's in the system at this point: Draft index: 3,840 main entries, 9,215 subentries, 21,470 page locators, 412 'see' and 'see also' cross-references. Book: 612 pages in 14 chapters plus notes (pp. 541–598) and bibliography. Each entry has heading, subentries, locators (single pages and ranges like 233–41), entry type (person, place, ship, concept), and count of locators. Known issues so far: 96 entries with more than 7 undifferentiated locators, the largest being 'whale oil' with 38. Chapter 9 (pp. 301–344) has about half the locator density of neighbouring chapters. 7 cross-references go to missing headings, and 1 loop runs 'sperm whaling' → 'whaling, sperm' → back. The publisher allows 28 typeset pages at about 110 lines per page, and the current estimate is 31.5 pages. The fee is $4.10 per indexable page.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
